factEarly: The littlest string instrument. You rub it with a bow!
factUpper: Held under the chin, its four strings are bowed or plucked. The shortest string plays the highest notes of the string family.

factEarly: You strum it with your fingers or a pick.
factUpper: Six strings are plucked or strummed. Frets on the neck shorten the strings to change pitch — the same idea as a violin fingerboard.

factEarly: A big string instrument you sit behind, like a hug!
factUpper: The cello sits between the player's knees, its endpin on the floor. Its long strings vibrate slowly, giving a rich, deep singing tone.

factEarly: The biggest string instrument — it goes super low!
factUpper: The largest and lowest string instrument. Its long, thick strings vibrate slowly, so players often stand or sit on a tall stool.

factEarly: You pluck its many strings with your fingers. So pretty!
factUpper: Forty-seven strings are plucked directly with the fingers. Shorter strings vibrate faster and play higher notes — no fingerboard needed.

factEarly: You blow air across a hole, like blowing across a bottle!
factUpper: The player blows air across the embouchure hole, splitting the stream to vibrate the air inside. It is one of the highest instruments in the orchestra.

factEarly: It has a reed that wiggles when you blow. Squawk!
factUpper: Air is split by a single reed tied to the mouthpiece. Covering and uncovering holes changes the length of the vibrating air column.

factEarly: It looks shiny like brass, but it is a woodwind — surprise!
factUpper: Made of brass but a woodwind: its sound comes from a single reed, like a clarinet. The bell and tube give it a bold, smooth voice.

factEarly: A giant woodwind with a bendy straw on top!
factUpper: A double-reed woodwind — two reeds vibrate against each other. Its folded tube is over 2.5 meters long, giving it a deep, reedy voice.

factEarly: Buzz your lips to play the shiny loud one!
factUpper: The player's lips buzz into the cup mouthpiece. Three valves open extra tubing to reach many notes. It is the highest brass instrument.

factEarly: It has a slide that goes wooOOOoo!
factUpper: Instead of valves, the trombone has a slide. Moving it in and out changes the tubing length, so players can glide between pitches.

factEarly: A coiled-up brass tube you wrap your hand inside!
factUpper: About 4 meters of tubing coiled into a circle. The player puts a hand inside the bell to shape the mellow sound and presses rotary valves.

factEarly: The giant brass one that goes super low — boom!
factUpper: The largest brass instrument, with the longest tube, so it plays the lowest notes. It takes lots of air to make its big, round sound.
Striking the top head shakes the drum; metal snares rattling against the bottom head give it its crisp buzz. Untuned — it keeps the rhythm.

factEarly: Giant copper bowls you tap with soft mallets. BOOM!
factUpper: Also called kettledrums. A pedal tightens or loosens the head to tune it to real pitches — rare for drums! Played with felt mallets.

factEarly: Wooden bars you bonk with mallets — like a wooden piano!
factUpper: Wooden bars of different sizes are struck with mallets. Short bars vibrate faster and sound higher — the same science as a piano's strings.

factEarly: A tiny metal triangle that goes ding! for a long time.
factUpper: A steel rod bent into a triangle, struck with a beater. The metal vibrates with many overtones, so its ring lasts a surprisingly long time.

factEarly: Little eggs full of tiny bits — shake shake shake!
factUpper: Sealed shells hold small beads. Shaking makes the beads bounce around inside, and all those tiny hits blend into one swishy sound.
